overview: Haakon VI of Norway was king of Norway and briefly Sweden, husband of Margaret I and father of Olaf IV. The profile is anchored by concrete turning points: 1343 — Becomes king of Norway; 1362 — Elected king of Sweden; 1363 — Marries Margaret.
He died in 1380, and his reign belongs to the wider story of Scandinavian state formation, Christianization, dynastic conflict, and northern Europe’s ties to England, the Baltic, and the Empire.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Haakon VI of Norway was born c. 1340. His family background is usually placed in Bjälbo / Norwegian royal line, though early Scandinavian genealogy can be uncertain and politically shaped.

Haakon VI of Norway's early life belonged to the medieval Scandinavian world, where kinship, sea routes, church contacts, assemblies, and armed followings shaped the opportunities available to a ruler.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Haakon VI of Norway is remembered less for a strongly drawn personality than for his pivotal place in Scandinavian dynastic politics, as the last king to rule Norway as a fully independent realm before the unions. The sources present a ruler engaged in the complex contests over the Norwegian and Swedish crowns, and above all for his marriage to Margaret I of Denmark — a union that would shape the entire future of the north.

His reign was spent navigating rivalry with the Mecklenburg claimants in Sweden and maintaining Norwegian autonomy under pressure, tasks that the record describes more in terms of events than of character. Through his son Olaf and his formidable wife, his dynastic line led directly to the Kalmar Union.

What survives is the impression of a ruler defined by his position in a dynastic web rather than by recorded temperament. He is remembered chiefly as Margaret's husband and as the last independent Norwegian king, his individual character largely overshadowed by the union politics he helped set in motion.

contentSections.title: As king of Norway and Sweden
paragraphs: Haakon VI inherited Norwegian kingship and became involved in Swedish politics through the conflicts around his father Magnus Eriksson. His marriage to Margaret I linked Norway and Denmark.
As King of Norway, King of Sweden, Haakon VI of Norway had to turn dynastic claim into workable authority through alliances, military pressure, church support, and acceptance by regional elites.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Died in Oslo in 1380, leaving Olaf IV as heir and Margaret I as the decisive political actor in Norway and Denmark.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: His legacy lies in the dynastic path that made Margaret’s Scandinavian union possible.
Later saga, saintly, or national traditions often amplified Haakon VI of Norway's reputation, so the article separates near-contemporary evidence from later memory where possible.
